readerTitle: Toyota's five whys: why the fuse was never the problem
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Toyota, 오노 다이이치의 기계 정지 사례) + 실제 연구 (5 Whys 비판) + 가상 적용 (배관 수리, 식당)
insight: 문제를 다시 일어나지 않게 하는 해결책은 처음 보이는 고장이 아니라, 원인을 몇 번 더 따라간 끝의 작고 값싼 공정 변경에 있는 경우가 많다.
misconception: 고장 난 부품을 바로 고치거나 더 튼튼한 것으로 바꾸면 문제는 해결된 것이다.

sources.text: Ohno, T. (1988). Toyota Production System: Beyond Large-Scale Production. Productivity Press. 일본어 원서 1978년. 기계 정지와 다섯 번의 '왜' 사례, 'Ask why five times' 원칙
Toyota Motor Corporation, Toyota Production System 소개 페이지 (jidoka, 이상 발생 시 라인 정지)
Card, A. J. (2017). The problem with '5 whys'. BMJ Quality & Safety, 26(8), 671–677.
배관 수리 회사와 식당 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 기계 정지 사례(과부하로 퓨즈 단선 → 베어링 윤활 부족 → 윤활 펌프 작동 불량 → 펌프 축 마모 → 스트레이너 미부착으로 금속 부스러기 유입)는 오노의 책 영문판에 나온 순서를 따랐습니다. 게시 전에 원문 표현을 다시 확인하세요.
오노가 이 방법을 실제로 쓴 정확한 연도와 공장은 확인하지 않았습니다. 그래서 카드에는 연도와 장소를 적지 않고 '오노가 책에서 설명한 사례'로만 썼습니다. 사키치 도요다가 기원이라는 설명도 확인 전이라 넣지 않았습니다.
작업자가 이상을 발견하면 라인을 멈출 수 있다는 내용(jidoka, andon)은 Toyota 공식 자료로 확인할 수 있습니다. 링크 주소가 지금도 유효한지 게시 전에 확인하세요.
Card(2017)의 서지 정보(권, 호, 쪽)를 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 연구 결과를 '한 줄의 원인만 따라가 다른 원인을 놓칠 수 있다'는 일반적인 비판으로만 요약했습니다.

cards.title: A machine stops. The fuse is blown.
body: Swap the fuse and the line is running again in minutes. Most factories would do exactly that and move on.
Taiichi Ohno, the engineer who shaped Toyota's production system, thought the fuse was the least interesting part of the story.

image.label: A stopped factory machine with a blown fuse
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 조용히 멈춘 공장 기계 옆에 끊어진 퓨즈 하나가 손바닥 위에 놓여 있음. 기계 뒤쪽에 작은 물음표 다섯 개가 그림자처럼 이어짐. 실제 자동차 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You run the line. What do you do?
body: A machine on your production line has stopped. A worker reports that it overloaded and the fuse blew.
Orders are waiting. What do you do?

options.text: Replace the fuse, restart, and log the stop
options.feedback: You get the line moving fast, which matters. But nothing has changed, so the same overload will likely blow the next fuse.

options.text: Fit a stronger fuse so it stops blowing
options.feedback: The stops end, but the overload doesn't. Now the fuse can't protect the machine, so a cheap part may turn into a broken motor.

options.text: Restart, then trace why it overloaded before closing the issue
options.feedback: It costs some time now. In return, you look for the cause that would make the stop come back. Next card shows where Ohno's chain led.

cards.title: Five questions, from fuse to strainer.
body: In his book on the Toyota Production System, Ohno walks through this exact stop:
list: **Why did it stop?** An overload blew the fuse.
**Why the overload?** A bearing wasn't lubricated enough.
**Why?** The lubrication pump wasn't pumping enough.
**Why?** The pump's shaft was worn and rattling.
**Why?** There was no strainer, so metal scraps got in.
cards.callout: The fix was attaching a strainer. A new fuse would have fixed nothing.

cards.title: Root cause, not symptom
body: A **root cause** is the deepest cause you can still act on. Fix it, and the problem stops coming back. A symptom is what you notice first: the blown fuse.
Ohno's habit was simple: **ask why five times**. Each answer becomes the next question. The number isn't magic. The point is to keep going past the first answer that lets you get back to work.

image.label: Chain from blown fuse down to missing strainer
image.brief: 위에서 아래로 내려가는 사슬 인포그래픽. 맨 위 "Fuse blew", 그 아래 "Bearing dry", "Pump weak", "Shaft worn", 맨 아래 "No strainer". 맨 위는 작고 흐리게, 맨 아래는 밝게 강조. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.softwareNote: A server crashes. Restarting it is the fuse. Asking why might lead to a full disk, then to logs that never get cleared, then to a setup step nobody owns. Many teams write this chain up after an outage.

cards.title: The system made stopping normal.
body: Toyota's production system lets workers stop the line when they spot a problem. That sounds expensive. The idea is that problems get looked at while the evidence is still fresh.
Ohno also stressed going to the machine itself instead of guessing from an office. The answers to each why came from looking at the real bearing, pump and shaft.
Asking why only works when people have the time, the access and the permission to find out.

cards.title: Now it's a plumbing business.
body: A plumbing company keeps getting called back for leaks it already fixed. The owner's first answer: "Some jobs just go wrong."
Asking why goes further. The fitting cracked. It was overtightened. Newer technicians judge tightness by feel. Training never covered it.
The root fix is a short guide and a ten-minute demo for new hires. It's cheaper than any number of free callbacks.

image.label: Plumber checking a fitting against a printed guide
image.brief: 플랫 일러스트. 싱크대 아래에서 배관공이 작은 체크카드를 보며 이음새를 조이는 장면. 배경에 달력에서 '재방문' 표시가 줄어드는 모습. 실제 브랜드나 로고 없음.

cards.title: One chain can miss the real story.
body: Problems often have several causes. Following one line of whys can make you stop at the first convincing story. Safety researchers in healthcare have criticized the method for exactly this.

Two other traps: stopping at "someone was careless," which blames a person instead of fixing a process, and answering from memory instead of going to look. If your chain ends in a person, ask one more why.

cards.title: Cold food on busy nights.
body: Your restaurant gets complaints about cold mains, mostly on Friday nights. You asked why twice and heard: "Plates sit at the pass." "Servers are too busy to grab them."

options.text: Remind servers to pick up plates faster
options.feedback: It's quick and free, but it stops at people. If something keeps servers busy, a reminder changes nothing by next Friday.

options.text: Hire another server for Friday nights
options.feedback: It may help, at a steady cost. But you'd be paying for a fix before knowing what's actually keeping servers busy.

options.text: Watch the floor next Friday and keep asking why servers are tied up
options.feedback: It costs a week. You might find something cheap, like drinks taking too long at a crowded bar, that a hire would only hide.

cards.title: Fix the thing that makes the problem come back.
body: The first answer gets you running again. The answer a few whys down keeps you running.
**Try it today:** pick a problem that has happened more than once. Write down why it happened, then ask why again until the answer is a process you can change.
